title: AI Engineering

nodes.label: ChatGPT: the name
nodes.desc: ChatGPT combines a chat interface with a Generative Pretrained Transformer.

nodes.label: Why ChatGPT took off
nodes.desc: Ease of use, a free tier, session memory, broad skill, viral sharing and good timing drove record adoption.

nodes.label: One model, many tasks
nodes.desc: The shift from training one specialist per task to a single general-purpose foundation model.

nodes.label: Why now: 4 ingredients
nodes.desc: Transformers, web-scale data, GPU compute and better training, all scaled together, enabled generative AI.

nodes.label: The AI race
nodes.desc: Intense competition among companies to release foundation models and assistants.

nodes.label: AI in the headlines
nodes.desc: Real-world impacts of AI on energy, misuse, user safety and jobs.

nodes.label: Next-token prediction
nodes.desc: The core task of a language model: output a probability distribution over the next token given the previous ones.

nodes.label: Autoregressive loop
nodes.desc: Text generation by repeatedly predicting a token, selecting it and appending it to the input.

nodes.label: Language model
nodes.desc: A model that assigns probabilities to word or token sequences, factorised into next-token probabilities by the chain rule.

nodes.label: LMs in speech recognition
nodes.desc: Using a language model to re-rank acoustically similar transcriptions by plausibility.

nodes.label: Self-supervised training
nodes.desc: Learning from raw text where the next word itself serves as the label, so no human annotation is needed.

nodes.label: Bigram model
nodes.desc: A counting-based model predicting the next word from only the previous word; its table grows as V squared.

nodes.label: Why prediction is powerful
nodes.desc: Architecture, training with alignment, and inference context together turn next-token prediction into capable behaviour.

nodes.label: Large language model
nodes.desc: A Transformer-based language model scaled up in data, parameters and compute; the text member of the foundation model family.

nodes.label: Emergent abilities
nodes.desc: Skills like translation, reasoning and coding that appear at scale from next-token training alone.

nodes.label: Foundation model
nodes.desc: A model trained on broad, large-scale data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks by prompting or fine-tuning.

nodes.label: AI system
nodes.desc: One or more models combined with context, data, tools, application logic and a user interface to solve a real task.

nodes.label: ChatGPT = FM+align+UI
nodes.desc: ChatGPT is a product: an aligned foundation model inside a chat interface with memory and safety filters.

nodes.label: FMs across modalities
nodes.desc: Foundation models for images, audio, video and multimodal data, such as CLIP, Whisper, Sora and Gemini.

nodes.label: AI engineering
nodes.desc: The discipline of building reliable, useful, maintainable applications with foundation models as core components.

nodes.label: AI engineering stack
nodes.desc: Six layers from application down to infrastructure, crossed by evaluation, safety and monitoring.

nodes.label: Capabilities to domains
nodes.desc: Six core AI capabilities that combine into many application domains.

nodes.label: Application archetypes
nodes.desc: Three common patterns: knowledge assistant, coding assistant and autonomous agent.

nodes.label: Demo vs system
nodes.desc: The gap between a one-off impressive demo and a reliable, safe, efficient production system.

nodes.label: Failure modes
nodes.desc: Ways an AI pipeline breaks, from outdated data and hallucinations to tool errors and prompt injection.

nodes.label: Code gen & vibe coding
nodes.desc: LLMs writing, debugging and translating code; vibe coding means building software mostly by prompting an AI.

nodes.label: Image & video generation
nodes.desc: Generative models like DALL-E 3 and Sora turning prompts into images and videos.

nodes.label: Open-weight models
nodes.desc: Models whose trained parameters are published under a license, without necessarily releasing code or data.

nodes.label: Ollama & llama.cpp
nodes.desc: Tools for downloading and running open-weight LLMs locally via CLI, GUI or HTTP server.

nodes.label: Weight memory
nodes.desc: Memory for model weights, roughly parameters times bits per weight divided by eight.

nodes.label: Model-fit challenge
nodes.desc: Hands-on exercise trading off model quality, memory use and generation speed on your own hardware.

nodes.label: LangChain & LangFlow
nodes.desc: A framework and its visual editor for composing prompts, chains, agents, memory and retrievers into LLM apps.

nodes.label: Course roadmap
nodes.desc: The course path: understand the models, build with models, engineer AI systems.

nodes.label: Lecture & lab
nodes.desc: Exam admission via a Jupyter-based computer lab with units on foundation models, agents, RAG and LoRA.

nodes.label: Research: efficient LLMs
nodes.desc: Research on quantisation such as BOF4, adapters, reasoning and neuromorphic hardware.

nodes.label: Text-to-Text Pipeline
nodes.desc: The six-stage path that turns input text into tokens, vectors, scores and finally new output text.

nodes.label: Pipeline Input Side
nodes.desc: Tokenization plus embedding lookup: the steps that convert a string into a sequence of vectors.

nodes.label: Pipeline Output Side
nodes.desc: Forward pass to logits, token selection and detokenization: the steps that turn vectors back into text.

nodes.label: Autoregressive Generation
nodes.desc: Generating text one token at a time, feeding each chosen token back in as input for the next step.

nodes.label: Token
nodes.desc: A discrete piece of text from a fixed vocabulary, identified by an integer ID; the unit an LLM reads and writes.

nodes.label: Vocabulary Granularity
nodes.desc: The choice of token size (character, subword or word), trading vocabulary size against sequence length.

nodes.label: Byte-Pair Encoding
nodes.desc: A greedy algorithm that builds a subword vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent token pair.

nodes.label: Byte-Level BPE
nodes.desc: BPE applied to UTF-8 bytes, starting from 256 byte tokens so any text can be encoded.

nodes.label: Tokenizer
nodes.desc: The component that converts text to token IDs and back, using a fixed vocabulary and merge rules.

nodes.label: Special Tokens
nodes.desc: Reserved control tokens such as start, end, padding and chat role markers.

nodes.label: Token Cost & Budget
nodes.desc: How token counts determine context usage, compute and API billing.

nodes.label: Tokenizer-Model Coupling
nodes.desc: A model is trained for one tokenizer; its output layer has one entry per vocabulary token.

nodes.label: Why IDs Need Embeddings
nodes.desc: Token IDs are arbitrary indices, so each is replaced by a learned vector that can carry meaning.

nodes.label: Embedding
nodes.desc: A learned d_model-dimensional vector for each token, stored as a row of the embedding matrix and fetched by ID.

nodes.label: One-Hot Projection
nodes.desc: Viewing embedding lookup as multiplying a sparse one-hot vector by the embedding matrix.

nodes.label: Embedding Geometry
nodes.desc: Learned embeddings place similar tokens near each other and encode relations as directions.

nodes.label: Norm vs. Direction
nodes.desc: Vector length tends to track word frequency, while vector direction carries meaning.

nodes.label: Cosine Similarity
nodes.desc: The cosine of the angle between two vectors, from -1 to +1, used to compare meaning independent of length.

nodes.label: Word2Vec (Skip-Gram)
nodes.desc: An early shallow network that learns word embeddings by predicting a word's context neighbours.

nodes.label: Static Token Embeddings
nodes.desc: The initial lookup gives each token the same vector regardless of its surrounding words.

nodes.label: Logits
nodes.desc: The raw score vector the model outputs at a position, one entry per vocabulary token.

nodes.label: Softmax
nodes.desc: A function that exponentiates and normalises scores into a probability distribution summing to one.

nodes.label: Generation Loop & Stopping
nodes.desc: Repeatedly score, select and append one token until <eos>, a length limit or a stop rule ends it.

nodes.label: Context Window
nodes.desc: The maximum number of tokens (prompt plus output) a model can process at once.

nodes.label: 5-Token Walkthrough
nodes.desc: A hand-run example of generation with a 5-token window that drops its oldest token when full.

nodes.label: Detokenization
nodes.desc: Turning generated token IDs back into text via their byte sequences and UTF-8 decoding.

nodes.label: Training Loop
nodes.desc: Next-token training: shift targets by one, compute cross-entropy, backpropagate and update weights.

nodes.label: Static vs Contextual
nodes.desc: Embeddings start identical for a token everywhere; contextual vectors adapt to the surrounding words.

nodes.label: Recurrence vs Attention
nodes.desc: Two ways to route information between positions: a step-by-step chain or weighted direct links.

nodes.label: RNN Forward Pass
nodes.desc: Each step embeds the token and mixes it with the previous hidden state through learned weights and a nonlinearity.

nodes.label: RNN Output Layer
nodes.desc: A linear layer maps the hidden state to logits, softmax gives probabilities, argmax picks a token.

nodes.label: Encoder-Decoder RNN
nodes.desc: An encoder compresses the input into a context vector that seeds a decoder generating the output.

nodes.label: Seq2Seq Translation Demo
nodes.desc: Step-by-step translation of 'I love machine learning' into Swedish with <bos> and <eos>.

nodes.label: Context Bottleneck
nodes.desc: One fixed-size vector cannot hold all details of long inputs, motivating attention.

nodes.label: Recurrent Neural Network
nodes.desc: A network that reads a sequence token by token, updating a hidden state that serves as memory.

nodes.label: Seq2Seq
nodes.desc: Encoder-decoder architecture that transforms one sequence into another of possibly different length.

nodes.label: Attention Scores
nodes.desc: Relevance numbers comparing the decoder state with each encoder state, via dot product or a learned additive function.

nodes.label: Weights & Context Vector
nodes.desc: Softmax-normalized scores used to average encoder states into a per-step context vector.

nodes.label: Decoder Update
nodes.desc: The decoder combines previous token, previous state and context vector to form its new state and output.

nodes.label: Attention Step by Step
nodes.desc: Walkthrough showing attention shifting across source words as each Swedish word is produced.

nodes.label: Attention Maps
nodes.desc: Heatmaps of attention weights, target by source, that reveal learned alignments.

nodes.label: Why Attention Helps
nodes.desc: Removes the bottleneck, shortens gradient paths and yields interpretable soft alignments.

nodes.label: Attention
nodes.desc: A mechanism that computes relevance weights and reads a weighted mix of representations from chosen positions.

nodes.label: Attention Is All You Need
nodes.desc: The 2017 paper that introduced the Transformer by dropping recurrence in favour of attention.

nodes.label: Cross- to Self-Attention
nodes.desc: Moving from attending to another sequence to attending within the same sequence.

nodes.label: Q, K, V Roles
nodes.desc: Query asks, key is matched, value is delivered - the library view of attention.

nodes.label: Q, K, V Projections
nodes.desc: Three learned matrices per layer that map each token vector to its query, key and value.

nodes.label: Scaled Dot-Product
nodes.desc: Match by dot product over sqrt(d_k), normalize by softmax, aggregate values.

nodes.label: Attention Matrix
nodes.desc: Matrix form softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V computing all positions at once; rows sum to one.

nodes.label: Multi-Head Attention
nodes.desc: Several attention heads with separate projections, concatenated and mixed by W_O.

nodes.label: Head Patterns
nodes.desc: Observed head behaviours like previous-token or coreference attention, learned rather than assigned.

nodes.label: Transformer
nodes.desc: Architecture built from stacked attention and feed-forward layers with residuals and normalization, without recurrence.

nodes.label: Self-Attention
nodes.desc: Attention in which every token of a sequence gathers information from tokens of the same sequence.

nodes.label: Queries, Keys, Values
nodes.desc: The three learned projections of each token used to match (query, key) and to carry information (value).

nodes.label: Multi-Head
nodes.desc: Running several attention operations in parallel so different relation types can be captured.

nodes.label: Permutation Equivariance
nodes.desc: Without position info, shuffling inputs to self-attention just shuffles its outputs.

nodes.label: Sinusoidal PE
nodes.desc: Fixed sine and cosine vectors at many frequencies added to embeddings to encode position.

nodes.label: PE Frequency Scales
nodes.desc: Fast waves in low dimensions give local position, slow waves in high dimensions give global position.

nodes.label: PE and Meaning
nodes.desc: Adding position shifts the embedding on purpose; the model learns to separate what from where.

nodes.label: Unmasked Attention
nodes.desc: Bidirectional encoder attention where each token sees all past and future tokens.

nodes.label: Causal Mask Matrix
nodes.desc: Adding minus infinity above the diagonal makes attention weights lower-triangular.

nodes.label: Parallel Train, Serial Gen
nodes.desc: Masked training predicts all positions at once, while inference appends one token at a time.

nodes.label: Positional Encoding
nodes.desc: Information about token position injected into the model so attention can use word order.

nodes.label: Causal Mask
nodes.desc: A mask that blocks attention to future positions so predictions depend only on the prefix.

nodes.label: Transformer Layer Parts
nodes.desc: Attention, FFN, residual connections and layer normalization arranged as MHA, Add & Norm, FFN, Add & Norm.

nodes.label: Position-wise FFN
nodes.desc: A two-layer network applied to each token separately, expanding 512 to 2048 and back.

nodes.label: Residual Connections
nodes.desc: Skip paths that add a sublayer's input to its output so it only learns an update.

nodes.label: LayerNorm & Add & Norm
nodes.desc: Per-token normalization with learned scale and shift, applied after each residual addition.

nodes.label: Stacking Layers
nodes.desc: Chaining L identical blocks so later layers build on features from earlier ones.

nodes.label: Width & Depth
nodes.desc: d_model and the number of layers, the two main knobs of model size.

nodes.label: Three Families
nodes.desc: Encoder-decoder, encoder-only and decoder-only Transformers and their typical tasks.

nodes.label: LM Head
nodes.desc: Linear layer mapping final hidden states to vocabulary logits; at generation only the last state is used.

nodes.label: Weight Tying
nodes.desc: Reusing the transposed embedding matrix as the output projection to halve those parameters.

nodes.label: Why Transformers Won
nodes.desc: Parallelism, direct connections and stable depth made Transformers replace RNNs.

nodes.label: Feed-Forward Network
nodes.desc: The per-token nonlinear sublayer of a Transformer block that transforms features within a token.

nodes.label: Residual & Norm
nodes.desc: Residual connections plus layer normalization that keep deep Transformer stacks trainable.

nodes.label: Pre-LN vs Post-LN
nodes.desc: Placement of normalization in a block; Pre-LN normalizes the sublayer input and keeps the residual path an identity.

nodes.label: RMSNorm
nodes.desc: Normalization that divides a token vector by its root mean square and applies a learned weight, without mean centering.

nodes.label: RoPE
nodes.desc: Rotary Position Embeddings: queries and keys are rotated by position-dependent angles so attention sees relative distance.

nodes.label: Multi-Query Attention
nodes.desc: Attention variant in which all query heads share a single key and value projection, minimizing the KV cache.

nodes.label: Grouped-Query Attention
nodes.desc: Query heads are split into groups that each share one key and value head; a tunable middle ground between MHA and MQA.

nodes.label: Gating & GLU
nodes.desc: A Gated Linear Unit multiplies a value projection by a sigmoid gate that controls how much of each feature passes.

nodes.label: SwiGLU FFN
nodes.desc: Feed-forward layer using a SiLU-gated linear unit that can both suppress and amplify features.

nodes.label: Modern Decoder Block
nodes.desc: Pre-RMSNorm, RoPE, grouped-query attention and a SwiGLU FFN on the classic attention-then-FFN skeleton.

nodes.label: KV Cache
nodes.desc: Store the keys and values of already-processed tokens per layer so each new token only computes its own query instead of re-running the whole prefix.

nodes.label: Mixture of Experts
nodes.desc: A layer that replaces the dense FFN with several expert FFNs plus a router, so each token runs only a few experts and gains capacity without more compute.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.desc: A learned gate that scores every expert for a token and selects the top-k, deciding which experts run and how their outputs are weighted.

nodes.label: Top-k Routing
nodes.desc: Selecting the k highest-scoring experts per token per layer; selection is discrete and reused by tokens that pick the same expert.

nodes.label: Expert FFN
nodes.desc: One of several interchangeable feed-forward networks inside a MoE layer, each with its own weights, applied only to tokens routed to it.

nodes.label: Active Parameters
nodes.desc: The subset of a model's parameters actually used to process one token, versus the total parameters stored, which include all experts.

nodes.label: Load Balancing
nodes.desc: An auxiliary training loss that encourages the router to spread tokens across experts instead of overusing a favoured few.

nodes.label: State Space Model
nodes.desc: A sequence model that keeps a fixed-size state, updated with linear maps as each token arrives, avoiding a growing KV cache.

nodes.label: Mamba
nodes.desc: A selective state space model whose update parameters depend on the input, so it can choose per token what to retain and write.

nodes.label: LSTM
nodes.desc: A recurrent network with a separate cell state and three gates (forget, input, output) that regulate memory over long spans.

nodes.label: Linear Attention
nodes.desc: Attention that folds past keys and values into one fixed-size matrix using a kernel feature map, giving linear cost in sequence length.

nodes.label: Gated DeltaNet
nodes.desc: Linear attention with a retention gate and error-driven updates that correct stale associations by writing only the delta.

nodes.label: Looped LLM
nodes.desc: A model that applies one shared block repeatedly, gaining processing steps without adding parameters, at the cost of latency.

nodes.label: xLSTM
nodes.desc: An extended LSTM with scalar and matrix memory that keeps recurrent gated memory competitive with attention.

nodes.label: Big-O Scaling
nodes.desc: How compute and memory grow with context length N for each architecture family, holding model size fixed.

nodes.label: Fixed-Size Memory
nodes.desc: A state of constant size that summarises the past, trading exact recall of specific tokens for memory that does not grow.

nodes.label: TTFT & TPOT
nodes.desc: Time to first token (prefill-sensitive) and time per output token (decode-sensitive), the two main latency metrics.

nodes.label: Architecture Choice
nodes.desc: Selecting a model family from application needs: retrieval accuracy, concurrent users, device memory and latency budget.

nodes.label: Training Data
nodes.desc: The text corpus an LLM learns from; its quality, coverage and mixture largely decide what the model can do.

nodes.label: Data Becomes Weights
nodes.desc: Next-token training stores the corpus's grammar, facts, style and task patterns in the weights; missing data means missing skills.

nodes.label: Data Sources
nodes.desc: Wikipedia, books, code, papers and above all web crawls such as Common Crawl make up pretraining corpora.

nodes.label: Crawlers & Transparency
nodes.desc: Company crawlers collect data whose composition is rarely disclosed; engineers must track provenance, licenses and privacy.

nodes.label: FineWeb
nodes.desc: Hugging Face's open 44 TB English web dataset built from 96 Common Crawl snapshots with a documented pipeline.

nodes.label: Cleaning Pipeline
nodes.desc: Staged processing: text extraction, URL blocklist, language filter, deduplication and heuristic quality filters.

nodes.label: Filtering & Dedup
nodes.desc: Filters reshape the data distribution; deduplication reduces memorization, and train-test overlap must be checked.

nodes.label: FineWeb-Edu
nodes.desc: Subset of FineWeb chosen by an LLM-trained classifier for educational value, giving better results with less data.

nodes.label: Data Mixing
nodes.desc: Choosing the token share of each source, upsampling valuable small sources and downsampling dominant ones.

nodes.label: Synthetic Data (Phi-1)
nodes.desc: Training text generated by another model, e.g. GPT-3.5-written textbooks used to train the Phi-1 code model.

nodes.label: Data Bias
nodes.desc: Models copy and can amplify skewed correlations in their corpus because they optimize likelihood, not truth or fairness.

nodes.label: Language Gap
nodes.desc: Performance differs by language, e.g. GPT-4 MMLU 85.5% in English vs 62.0% in Telugu.

nodes.label: Pretraining
nodes.desc: Self-supervised next-token training on a large corpus; there is no human labeling because the text shifts itself into targets.

nodes.label: Cross-Entropy Loss
nodes.desc: The negative log probability the model gives the correct next token; low probability means high loss.

nodes.label: FLOPs
nodes.desc: Floating-point operations measuring training compute; about 6 per parameter per token for dense autoregressive LLMs.

nodes.label: Pretraining Objective
nodes.desc: Predict the next token given all previous ones, trained in parallel across positions with causal masking.

nodes.label: LR Schedules
nodes.desc: Linear warm-up to a peak followed by cosine decay, keeping Adam's updates stable and converging smoothly.

nodes.label: Training Batches
nodes.desc: The set of token sequences whose gradients combine into one optimizer update; B * L tokens per batch.

nodes.label: Training Hardware
nodes.desc: GPUs such as the H100 provide parallel matrix math, high bandwidth and fast interconnects that make pretraining feasible.

nodes.label: Numeric Precision
nodes.desc: The numeric format of weights, activations, gradients and optimizer states; it controls stability, memory, speed and feasible model size.

nodes.label: Parallelism
nodes.desc: Distributing training across GPUs with data, tensor and pipeline strategies, combined with ZeRO sharding of training states.

nodes.label: Single-GPU Limit
nodes.desc: Large models, gradients, optimizer states and activations exceed one GPU's memory and compute, forcing distribution.

nodes.label: Gradient Accumulation
nodes.desc: Summing gradients over N micro-batches to apply one averaged update, simulating a large batch within limited memory.

nodes.label: Data Parallelism
nodes.desc: Each GPU holds the full model and different data; gradients are averaged so all replicas update identically.

nodes.label: Tensor Parallelism
nodes.desc: Splitting individual weight matrices across GPUs, combining partial outputs, at the cost of frequent communication.

nodes.label: Pipeline Parallelism
nodes.desc: Assigning groups of consecutive layers to different GPUs and streaming micro-batches through the stages.

nodes.label: ZeRO / FSDP
nodes.desc: ZeRO shards optimizer states, gradients and parameters across data-parallel GPUs; PyTorch FSDP implements this style.

nodes.label: Choosing Parallelism
nodes.desc: Matching each technique to its bottleneck and combining them to balance memory, throughput and communication.

nodes.label: Base Model
nodes.desc: Pretraining's output: a decoder-only Transformer that continues text but is not yet aligned; e.g. Llama 3.1 8B.

nodes.label: Training Recipe
nodes.desc: The coordinated plan of data mixture, data schedule and optimization settings across training phases that shapes a model's capabilities.

nodes.label: OLMo 2
nodes.desc: A 7B model trained in stages: ~4T tokens broad pretraining, then three 50B-token midtraining runs averaged element-wise.

nodes.label: Context Extension
nodes.desc: Growing the context window in stages, e.g. Llama 3's 8K -> 128K over six stages with ~800B extra tokens.

nodes.label: Domain Upsampling
nodes.desc: Raising the sampling probability of chosen domains, e.g. math and code in the final 20% of training, shifting capabilities.

nodes.label: Data Scheduling
nodes.desc: Deciding when each kind of data appears during training: uniform mixing, or changing the mixture over time (curriculum).

nodes.label: Scaling Laws
nodes.desc: Empirical power-law formulas linking held-out loss to model size, training data and compute, used to plan budgets and forecast performance.

nodes.label: Kaplan Power Law
nodes.desc: 2020 fit of loss to non-embedding parameters with exponent ~0.076; doubling size cuts loss about 5.1%.

nodes.label: Compute C = 6ND
nodes.desc: Dense-Transformer training compute is about six times parameters times tokens, from forward and backward FLOPs.

nodes.label: Chinchilla
nodes.desc: 2022 study showing model size and tokens should grow about equally with compute, correcting earlier over-sizing.

nodes.label: ~20 Tokens per Param
nodes.desc: Compute-optimal rule of thumb: about twenty training tokens per parameter.

nodes.label: Overtraining
nodes.desc: Training beyond the compute-optimal token count so a smaller model is cheaper to serve; not the same as overfitting.

nodes.label: Scaling Limits
nodes.desc: Data quality, repetition, architecture and recipe break the fit; extrapolation is risky and deployment picks on more than loss.

nodes.label: In-Context Learning
nodes.desc: Learning a new task from prompt examples at inference time, without updating any weights.

nodes.label: Base Model Continuation
nodes.desc: A pretrained base model only continues text plausibly; it does not follow instructions or answer questions.

nodes.label: Few-Shot Prompting
nodes.desc: Example pairs in the prompt define the task and constrain the output format by pattern continuation.

nodes.label: Algorithmic vs Semantic
nodes.desc: Two ICL modes: mechanical pattern skills from attention, and task inference from stored world knowledge.

nodes.label: Induction Heads
nodes.desc: Attention circuits that find an earlier match and copy its successor, the mechanism behind algorithmic ICL.

nodes.label: Limits of ICL
nodes.desc: ICL is statistical continuation: picky about format and examples, with no correctness or safety guarantee.

nodes.label: Post-Training
nodes.desc: The second stage after pretraining that shapes a base model into a helpful, instruction-following assistant.

nodes.label: Supervised Fine-Tuning
nodes.desc: Continued next-token training on human-written instruction-response pairs to teach instruction following.

nodes.label: InstructGPT
nodes.desc: SFT plus RLHF with ~13,000 examples from ~40 annotators; the shift from base models to assistants.

nodes.label: ChatGPT Stack
nodes.desc: A product = foundation model + alignment (tuning + RLHF) + interface with memory and safety filters.

nodes.label: Limits of SFT
nodes.desc: Imitation with no notion of better or worse: no negative signal, fluency over truth, style overfitting.

nodes.label: Preference Is Hard
nodes.desc: Many topics have no universally correct answer; culture, politics and identity make a single universal preference impossible to encode.

nodes.label: Absolute vs Relative
nodes.desc: Absolute 1-7 scores are noisy and hackable; pairwise comparisons and rankings are stable and preferred.

nodes.label: Preference Dataset
nodes.desc: Diverse prompts with sampled candidate answers ranked by humans, decomposed into (x, y_w, y_l) triples.

nodes.label: RL Basics
nodes.desc: Learning by acting and receiving rewards; in RLHF the LLM is the agent, prompts the state and text the action.

nodes.label: Reward Model
nodes.desc: A base-architecture model with a scalar head that scores answers, trained with the Bradley-Terry logistic loss.

nodes.label: RLHF
nodes.desc: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model, then optimize the SFT model, typically with PPO.

nodes.label: PPO + KL Penalty
nodes.desc: RLHF optimization that maximizes reward while a beta-weighted KL penalty keeps the policy near the SFT reference.

nodes.label: DPO
nodes.desc: Direct Preference Optimization: a closed-form loss on preference pairs, with the policy's log-ratio as an implicit reward, no RL.

nodes.label: Why Decoding Matters
nodes.desc: The rule that turns the long-tailed next-token distribution into an actual token, controlling determinism, creativity, safety and hallucination risk.

nodes.label: Stable Softmax (Log-Sum-Exp)
nodes.desc: Subtracting the maximum logit before softmax avoids overflow to inf or NaN while leaving probabilities unchanged.

nodes.label: Greedy Decoding
nodes.desc: Always pick the argmax token; deterministic and fast but repetitive and prone to error snowballing.

nodes.label: Random Sampling
nodes.desc: Draw a token in proportion to its probability using cumulative probabilities and a uniform random number.

nodes.label: Temperature
nodes.desc: Divide logits by T before softmax: T < 1 sharpens (more deterministic), T > 1 flattens (more random).

nodes.label: Top-k Sampling
nodes.desc: Keep only the k most probable tokens, renormalize and sample; fixed k can be too strict or too loose.

nodes.label: Top-p Sampling
nodes.desc: Keep the smallest token set whose cumulative probability reaches p and sample; the set adapts to the distribution.

nodes.label: Comparing Strategies
nodes.desc: Greedy is safe and factual, temperature tunable, top-k medium, top-p high-diversity for open-ended tasks.

nodes.label: Why and How We Evaluate
nodes.desc: Continuous testing of quality, reliability, safety and fit at three levels: intrinsic, task-level and practical capability.

nodes.label: Perplexity
nodes.desc: Exponential of the cross-entropy loss; the effective number of choices the model is uncertain among. Lower is better.

nodes.label: Accuracy, BLEU, ROUGE
nodes.desc: Task-level scores: accuracy for classification, BLEU (precision) for translation, ROUGE (recall) for summarisation.

nodes.label: Pass@k for Code
nodes.desc: Probability that at least one of k generated samples passes the unit tests, used for code generation.

nodes.label: Benchmarks
nodes.desc: Standardized task suites with a fixed scoring rule so that model scores are comparable across releases and teams.

nodes.label: MMLU Knowledge Benchmark
nodes.desc: 57-subject multiple-choice knowledge and reasoning test scored by accuracy; below 50% is under undergraduate, ~95% expert.

nodes.label: BIG-Bench Suite
nodes.desc: About 200 community tasks probing logic, reasoning and off-distribution skills; no single score, reveals emergent abilities.

nodes.label: HumanEval Benchmark
nodes.desc: 164 hand-written Python tasks graded by hidden unit tests and reported as pass@k.

nodes.label: Long-Horizon Reasoning
nodes.desc: Multi-step dependent tasks scored by pass rate; benchmarks include SWE-bench and Aider Polyglot.

nodes.label: Safety & Factuality
nodes.desc: Toxicity, bias, jailbreak, privacy, plus hallucination and deception checks such as FActScore.

nodes.label: Multi-Turn Instruction
nodes.desc: Holding instructions and constraints across many turns; shaped by SFT/RLHF, not classical metrics.

nodes.label: Tool Use & Tau-2 Bench
nodes.desc: Schema-correct tool calls and agent tasks across retail, airline and telecom in a dual-control setting.

nodes.label: Modality & Domain Evals
nodes.desc: Multimodal tests (VQA, ChartQA, VideoMME) and high-stakes domain tests (HealthBench, LegalEval, GSM8K).

nodes.label: Benchmark Limitations
nodes.desc: Contamination and saturation inflate scores; no single number captures quality, so test many dimensions.

nodes.label: Prompt Engineering
nodes.desc: Adapting a model's behaviour through input text alone, without changing any weights.

nodes.label: Prompt First, Then Finetune
nodes.desc: The principle of pushing prompting to its limit before spending effort on finetuning or retrieval.

nodes.label: System Prompt
nodes.desc: The highest-priority role that sets global rules, persona, tone and constraints for a chat model.

nodes.label: Role Hierarchy
nodes.desc: System beats user beats assistant history; learned during alignment and essential for safety and consistency.

nodes.label: Zero-Shot Prompting
nodes.desc: Giving the model only an instruction, no examples, relying on pretraining and alignment.

nodes.label: Zero-Shot Trade-offs
nodes.desc: Fast and strong on simple tasks, a good baseline, but weak on specialised or ambiguous ones.

nodes.label: Few-Shot Prompting
nodes.desc: Placing a few solved examples in the prompt so the model infers the pattern via in-context learning.

nodes.label: Few-Shot Tips
nodes.desc: Short, clean, well-ordered examples help; examples cost context and can be copied too literally.

nodes.label: Chain-of-Thought
nodes.desc: Asking the model to reason step by step before answering, boosting maths, logic and planning.

nodes.label: CoT Emergence
nodes.desc: The step-by-step benefit unlocks mainly in large models, evidence of an emergent ability.

nodes.label: CoT Properties
nodes.desc: One autoregressive pass, no internal planner; more accurate but slower and not real subtask solving.

nodes.label: Context Management
nodes.desc: Deciding what enters the context window and how it is structured so the model reasons well.

nodes.label: Lost in the Middle
nodes.desc: Primacy and recency biases give a U-shaped attention profile; the middle is a weak dead zone.

nodes.label: Chunking & Summarization
nodes.desc: Splitting documents at natural boundaries and compressing history into short task-focused summaries.

nodes.label: Pruning & Reiteration
nodes.desc: Deleting noisy turns to stabilise output, and repeating critical rules at the end of the context.

nodes.label: Prompt Ordering
nodes.desc: Placing rules, instructions, examples and the task in the order the model attends to best.

nodes.label: Context Challenges
nodes.desc: Finite windows, growing latency and drifting behaviour that make context management necessary.

nodes.label: Instruction & Persona
nodes.desc: Direct task commands and role-play personas that shape tone, expertise and style.

nodes.label: Example & CoT
nodes.desc: Few-shot demonstrations and step-by-step reasoning patterns for mappings, structure and logic.

nodes.label: Critique & Self-Check
nodes.desc: Self-evaluating and self-correcting patterns that reduce errors and improve quality.

nodes.label: Decomposition
nodes.desc: Breaking hard tasks into steps, subtasks, expert roles or pseudo-code modules.

nodes.label: Tree-of-Thought
nodes.desc: Branching into several candidate strategies, scoring them and picking the best; plus problem rewriting.

nodes.label: Style & Hard Rules
nodes.desc: Controlling tone and voice, and enforcing explicit must-follow output rules.

nodes.label: Soft Steering & Guardrails
nodes.desc: Gently nudging behaviour or combining style and rules to block unsafe output.

nodes.label: Structured Output
nodes.desc: Forcing the model to answer in a fixed schema such as JSON so downstream code can parse it reliably.

nodes.label: Function Calling
nodes.desc: Letting the model trigger external tools via schemas, offloading maths and search to real systems.

nodes.label: Prompt vs Native Tools
nodes.desc: Tool schemas as system-prompt text for open models, or on a separate trained channel for closed APIs.

nodes.label: get_weather Example
nodes.desc: A weather tool declared with a JSON schema whose required city string is filled by the model's tool call.

nodes.label: Prompt Failure Modes
nodes.desc: Common failure types: hallucination, ignored constraints, style drift, wrong reasoning, wrong length, unstable output.

nodes.label: Improve & Test
nodes.desc: Fixing a prompt with explicit rules, role, examples and structure, then testing phrasings and edge cases.

nodes.label: Why Automate Prompts
nodes.desc: Hand-written prompts are slow and inconsistent; optimization treats prompting as a search problem.

nodes.label: The APO Loop
nodes.desc: Generate prompt variants by mutation and crossover, score them with metrics, keep the best, repeat until convergence.

nodes.label: Parametric vs Non-Parametric
nodes.desc: Weights are static, opaque and stale; RAG injects external, updatable facts at inference time.

nodes.label: RAG
nodes.desc: Generation conditioned on the query plus retrieved evidence, p(y | x, RAG(x)); retrieval is an information bottleneck.

nodes.label: RAG Pipeline
nodes.desc: Offline chunk-embed-store plus online embed-search-rerank-assemble-generate.

nodes.label: RAG vs Alignment
nodes.desc: Alignment decides how to answer; RAG decides what to answer with; they are complementary.

nodes.label: Hallucinations & RAG
nodes.desc: RAG grounds answers and reduces hallucination, moving failure from fabrication to retrieval quality.

nodes.label: Embedding Models
nodes.desc: Maps text into R^d (e.g. 384, 768, 1536) so similar meanings sit close; retrieval becomes nearest-neighbor search.

nodes.label: Sentence-BERT & Pooling
nodes.desc: BERT plus pooling collapses token vectors into one sentence vector: mean, max, [CLS] or weighted.

nodes.label: Siamese Bi-Encoder
nodes.desc: Two shared-weight BERT towers with a contrastive, cosine-based loss; enables precomputed document embeddings.

nodes.label: Embedding Model Types
nodes.desc: General-purpose, domain-adapted and cross-lingual models, plus instruction-tuned and asymmetric encoders.

nodes.label: Chunking
nodes.desc: Splits documents into contiguous segments (200-500 tokens, often with overlap) as the atomic unit of RAG knowledge.

nodes.label: Contextual Retrieval
nodes.desc: An LLM prepends a short document-level context to each chunk before embedding, making it self-contained.

nodes.label: Embedding Quality & Recall
nodes.desc: Embedding quality sets the recall ceiling; chunks that are not near the query can never be retrieved.

nodes.label: Vector Store
nodes.desc: Stores embeddings and retrieves by similarity, offering ANN search and metadata filtering instead of exact keys.

nodes.label: ANN Search
nodes.desc: Approximate nearest-neighbor search: a structured index inspects a small subset, trading exactness for speed.

nodes.label: IVF Index
nodes.desc: Clusters vectors with k-means and searches only the clusters nearest the query; recall depends on clusters probed.

nodes.label: Quantization
nodes.desc: Compresses vectors into codebooks (PQ, scalar) to cut memory and speed access, with a small recall loss.

nodes.label: FAISS & Index Comparison
nodes.desc: Open-source ANN library with Flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ, IVF-PQ; indexes trade memory, recall and speed.

nodes.label: NSW: Building
nodes.desc: Insert nodes with greedy search, then pick up to M edges preferring close, diverse neighbors.

nodes.label: NSW: Searching
nodes.desc: Greedy walk from a random entry toward more similar nodes until a local best; return top-k visited.

nodes.label: Skip List
nodes.desc: Stacked linked lists with sparser upper levels; move to local best per level, then drop down.

nodes.label: HNSW
nodes.desc: NSW graphs layered like a skip list: search the sparse top, descend and refine; the RAG default.

nodes.label: Dense Retrieval
nodes.desc: Returns top-k chunks by cosine similarity in a shared vector space; semantic but weak on exact IDs and strings.

nodes.label: BM25
nodes.desc: Rule-based sparse ranking with IDF, term-frequency saturation and length normalization; exact-keyword strength.

nodes.label: Hybrid Retrieval
nodes.desc: Runs dense and sparse retrieval, fuses the ranked lists, then reranks or generates for greater robustness.

nodes.label: RRF
nodes.desc: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: sums 1/(k + rank) over lists, scale-invariant, with a single smoothing constant k of about 60.

nodes.label: Why Cache Keys and Values?
nodes.desc: During generation the model predicts each new token from the prompt plus everything generated so far.

nodes.label: Prefill and Decode
nodes.desc: Inference runs in two phases.

nodes.label: Where the Latency Goes
nodes.desc: Total response time is the prefill time plus one decode step for every further output token.

nodes.label: Sizing the KV Cache
nodes.desc: The cache stores, per sequence, per layer and per cached position, one key vector and one value vector for every KV head.

nodes.label: Capacity, Quantization and B
nodes.desc: With everything else fixed, the cache grows with cached positions, concurrent sequences, attention layers, KV heads and bytes per element.

nodes.label: Batching and Memory Bandwidt
nodes.desc: A server can batch requests from several users so that each decode step processes one new position per sequence on the same model instance.

nodes.label: Levers to Shrink the Cache
nodes.desc: You can shrink the cache along three axes.

nodes.label: More Capacity, Same Compute
nodes.desc: In a dense Transformer the same feed-forward network processes every token in every layer.

nodes.label: Conditional Computation: Den
nodes.desc: Conditional computation lets a network hold more parameters than it uses for any single input, by choosing which components to run based on that input.

nodes.label: Experts, Router, Combination
nodes.desc: A sparse MoE layer replaces the dense FFN sublayer of a Transformer block with several feed-forward networks, called experts, plus a learned router.

nodes.label: Inside the Router
nodes.desc: The router multiplies the token representation by a learned router matrix, giving one score per expert.

nodes.label: Combining Expert Outputs
nodes.desc: Each selected expert is a separate feed-forward network that receives the same token representation and transforms it with its own weights, so different experts.

nodes.label: How Router and Experts Learn
nodes.desc: Router and experts are trained jointly from the ordinary next-token prediction loss, with no predefined topic labels telling experts what to specialise in.

nodes.label: Shared and Fine-Grained Expe
nodes.desc: Two design choices refine the basic MoE layer.

nodes.label: Efficiency: Compute, Memory,
nodes.desc: Sparse activation affects resources differently.

nodes.label: MoE in Practice
nodes.desc: Publicly documented models use MoE in different ways.

nodes.label: Why Look Beyond Attention
nodes.desc: Self-attention lets every token look back at all earlier tokens, but that explicit access is expensive: the KV cache grows with the sequence and each new token .

nodes.label: Recurrence Without Sequentia
nodes.desc: Recurrent models pass information from one token to the next, which seems to force strictly sequential computation.

nodes.label: Hybrid: Nemotron 3 Nano
nodes.desc: Real models increasingly mix mechanisms.

nodes.label: What Big-O Hides
nodes.desc: Two models with the same Big-O can perform very differently on real hardware.

nodes.label: What Fixed-Size Memory Gives
nodes.desc: Full attention keeps token-specific keys and values, so a later question can directly attend to an earlier detail, although correct retrieval is still not guara.

nodes.label: Prefill vs Decode Performanc
nodes.desc: Inference has two phases with different bottlenecks.

nodes.label: Ways to Spend the Model Budg
nodes.desc: Architects trade capacity, active computation, memory and information access in different ways.

nodes.label: Choosing an Architecture
nodes.desc: There is no universally best architecture; the choice follows application requirements.

demo.welcome_say: Welcome to the AI Engineering course. In this tour you will travel from raw text to tokens, through attention and training, all the way to retrieval and prompt engineering.

demo.tour_end: That was the AI Engineering course overview. Each chapter is a full lesson with cards, labs and a quiz.

category_say.Intro: Chapter 1, Introduction & AI Engineering. Explain what ChatGPT is, why it spread so fast, and which shift and ingredients made general-purpose generative AI possible.
category_say.Tokens: Chapter 2, From Text to Tokens and Back. Trace how a sentence travels through an LLM system, from raw text to token IDs, vectors, scores and back to text, one token at a time.
category_say.LLM Foundations: Chapter 3, Foundations of LLMs. Understand how recurrent networks turn a token sequence into context-aware hidden states, how an encoder-decoder maps one sequence to another, and why a single fixed context vector becomes a bottleneck.
category_say.Training: Chapter 4, Training & Alignment. Understand where LLM training text comes from, how raw web crawls are turned into clean, well-mixed corpora, and how data choices shape model quality and bias.
category_say.Inference: Chapter 5, Inference & Evaluation. Explain how a model's next-token probabilities are turned into actual text, and how greedy, sampling, temperature, top-k and top-p trade determinism against creativity.
category_say.Prompting: Chapter 6, Prompt Engineering. Understand what prompt engineering is and how system, user and assistant roles shape a chat model's behaviour.
category_say.RAG: Chapter 7, Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Explain why parametric language models need external knowledge and how Retrieval-Augmented Generation supplies it.
